extracted.intended_audience: small law firms and SMMEs in South Africa
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on intellectual property (GIs, TK/TCE, ABS, patents and related regulation) for small law firms and small, medium and micro enterprises operating in South Africa. Covers statutory requirements, permit and disclosure obligations, international instruments, and practical enforcement/labeling rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for registration (South African GI)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three elements required to be present: The product must be linked to or originate from a specific location; The product must possess a unique quality or characteristic; There must be a link between the quality and location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three elements are the substantive tests for registration as a South African geographical indication (GI) (see Section 17 of the GI regulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: GI validity period
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs are valid for an indefinite period until the registration is cancelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from other IPRs, such as trade marks, which are valid for a 10-year period although can be renewed on application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labelling foodstuffs using registered GIs as ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: A name registered as a South African GI or foreign GI, including those protected under FTAs, may be used as part of or near the product name, such as on labels or in advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usage is subject to strict requirements outlined in the GI regulations (i.e., permitted but regulated — consult the GI regulations for specific labelling rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquor Products Act restrictions on geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: The Minister of Agriculture can restrict the use of geographical names relating to the sale and export of liquor products; EU GIs are protected under this Act as published in the government gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the cited government notices (e.g., Notice R40382 of 28 October 2016 and Notice R4536 of 22 March 2024) for the list and scope of protected names under the LPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade Marks Act — GIs as collective or certification marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trade Marks Act provides for the registration of a GI in the form of a collective or certification mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants can seek protection via trade mark registration routes (collective or certification marks) in addition to GI-specific registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement and offences for unauthorised GI use
rubrics_metrics.description: The unauthorised use of GIs constitutes an offence, in which rights are enforceable by the holder of the right; improper use of prohibited marks, collective and certification marks registered as a trade mark may also constitute an act of counterfeiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departmental roles: DALRRD enforces APSA and the GI Regulations and the LPA; the dtic administers and enforces non-compliance with the MMA (prohibited marks). Enforcement actions and criminal/civil remedies may follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: GI protection by agreement (FTAs/EPAs)
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs may be protected by international or regional agreements (FTAs/EPAs) — e.g., the SADC‑EU EPA lists protected GIs in Annex 1 of Protocol 3 and protects against misuse, imitation and commercial use; SACUM‑UK EPA and bilateral agreements likewise provide protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection under such agreements is achieved by listing names in treaty annexes and by implementing those commitments in domestic law; details and lists are in the specific protocol annexures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territoriality and international protection of GIs
rubrics_metrics.description: GI rights are territorial and are limited to the country or region where the protection is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GIs can be protected nationally (each country separately), regionally (e.g., OAPI, ARIPO) or internationally via the WIPO Lisbon system; consult the relevant system for filing/coverage rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent applications involving Traditional Knowledge (TK) — declaration and proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patents Act requires the applicant for a patent to include a declaration of whether the patent is derived from TK or the use of TK, and whether the invention is based on or derived from an indigenous biological or genetic resource.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If declared to derive from TK or its use, the Commissioner of Patents must call for proof of the applicant’s rights to use the TK; in the absence of such proof, the patent application will not be registered (see Section 30(3A) and Form P.26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of current IP systems for TK and TCE
rubrics_metrics.description: While the current international patent system is appropriate for protecting innovations based on TK, it does not provide protection for TK as such; TCE (traditional cultural expressions) can be protected by existing IP systems such as copyright, related rights, geographical indications, trade marks, and designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO is working on new international legal instruments to better protect TK and TCE; practitioners should be aware current protections are piecemeal and instrument-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Property Law Amendment Act (IPLAA) provisions on indigenous knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: IPLAA provides for the protection of certain types of Indigenous knowledge as a species of intellectual property rights and amends Acts (Copyright Act, Performers’ Protection Act, Trade Mark Act, Designs Act) to include recognition/registration of indigenous works, performances, terms/expressions and designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPLAA also provides for establishment of a National Council for Indigenous knowledge, a National Database for IKS (kept with existing IP registers), and a National Trust and Fund. Note: IPLAA has been assented to but had not come into effect pending regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection, Promotion, Development and Management of Indigenous Knowledge Act (IK Act) and NIKSO
rubrics_metrics.description: The IK Act's primary objective is to protect Indigenous knowledge from unauthorised use and to regulate fair and equitable distribution of benefits from its commercial use through the National Indigenous Knowledge Systems Office (NIKSO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIKSO (and the IK Registration System/NIKMAS) supports communities to record IK; accessing the IK Registration System requires permission and authorisation. The IK Act was assented to but awaits proclamation and regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: WIPO Treaty (2024) — disclosure of origin/source in patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (adopted May 2024) contains provisions regarding the disclosure of origin/source of genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge in patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaty is not yet in force (requires 15 ratifications); it addresses disclosure obligations but does not itself create ABS rules — monitor ratification and national implementing measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABS fundamentals and Nagoya Protocol obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) covers how genetic resources may be accessed and how users and providers agree on fair sharing of benefits; the general ABS principles are contained in the CBD and elaborated in the Nagoya Protocol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Nagoya Protocol creates predictable conditions for access, helps ensure benefit-sharing when genetic resources leave the provider country, and sets out core obligations for contracting parties regarding access, benefit-sharing and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: South African ABS legislation and permit requirements (NEMBA & BABS)
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa implements ABS through domestic legislation, notably the National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act (NEMBA) and the Bioprospecting, Access and Benefit Sharing Regulations (BABS) which govern commercial exploitation, discovery and commercialisation phases and set form/content/requirements for benefit-sharing and material transfer agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A permit is required for anyone carrying out bioprospecting involving indigenous biological resources and for anyone exporting indigenous biological resources for bioprospecting or research. A permit will only be issued if there is material disclosure to stakeholders, prior informed consent has been obtained, and the Minister is satisfied that statutory conditions have been met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder categories and agreement requirements for bioprospecting
rubrics_metrics.description: Two categories of stakeholders are those who gave access to the indigenous biological resources (e.g., land owner) and indigenous communities whose knowledge or traditional use has contributed to the bioprospecting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefit-sharing agreements must be entered into with stakeholders, and a material transfer agreement must be entered into with stakeholders who give access to the indigenous biological resources. BABS Regulations include a benefit-sharing agreement template (Appendix 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: DEA role and guidance for ABS permits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department of Environmental Affairs (DEA) acts as the clearing house and focal point for ABS in South Africa and administers NEMBA and BABS; it provides guidelines to assist stakeholders in understanding legal requirements and securing required permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the DEA guidelines when planning commercial bioprospecting; the DEA guide assists in completing bioprospecting permit applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biodiversity Bill proposed changes affecting ABS and bioprospecting
rubrics_metrics.description: The draft National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Bill (published for comment in 2024) proposes amendments including a revised regulatory approach, provisions on listing species and ecosystems, implementation of international agreements, wildlife tracking, a complete revision of bioprospecting and ABS provisions, and stricter penalties for offences by State officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once enacted the Bill will repeal NEMBA and contains transitional arrangements to facilitate transition from NEMBA provisions to the new measures; stakeholders should monitor progress and adapt compliance practices accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABS Clearing-House (ABSCH) and information-sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABS Clearing-House (ABSCH) is a platform established by the Nagoya Protocol to share information on ABS, providing users access to genetic resources and associated TK and helping providers fairly and equitably share in benefits from utilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ABSCH as a key tool for implementation of Nagoya obligations and for locating information relevant to access/benefit-sharing arrangements.
